title: TeeVee Toons, Inc. v. Gerhard Schubert GmbH
summary: Under the CISG, a factual dispute about the parties’ intent to exclude printed terms—including their merger clause—prevented summary judgment based on those terms.
notes:
It supplies a denial of part of the seller’s summary-judgment request, not a final award to the buyer. The complete CISG and its applicability exceptions are not reproduced in this supplement.

The case (S.D.N.Y. Aug. 23, 2006, 2006 WL 2463537) is usually taught for the point that, unlike the UCC parol evidence rule, CISG Article 8 lets a court consider evidence of the negotiations that contradicts the written terms, so a merger clause and warranty disclaimer do not automatically control.

sections.Parties: TeeVee Toons and its affiliate developed the Biobox, a biodegradable cassette package. German manufacturer Gerhard Schubert GmbH contracted to build the production system, dealing through its United States agent Rodico.
sections.Material Facts:
After negotiations, the parties entered a written quotation contract in February 1995 for machinery to manufacture the Biobox rapidly and reliably. Delivery was delayed nearly two years, and the system then malfunctioned seriously. The buyer alleged that the machinery was unfit for its ordinary and particular purposes and gave notice of nonconformity. The manufacturer relied on attached terms limiting warranties and liability.

The buyer’s representative testified that, before acceptance, the seller’s agent assured him that the fine print was meaningless for this project and could be ignored. The agent admitted telling the buyer not to worry about or overemphasize the fine print, but disputed the stronger wording. The disputed boilerplate itself included an entire-agreement clause purporting to supersede prior understandings. The seller sought to cap recovery at the machinery price and restrict the warranties otherwise supplied by the CISG.
sections.Procedural History: The plaintiffs sued in 2000; an earlier dismissal motion was denied. In 2006 the Southern District of New York ruled on Schubert’s summary-judgment motion. The reproduced portion denied judgment on the Article 35(2)(a)–(b) contract claim, except as to specified categories of damages addressed in omitted material. It did not finally decide whose factual account was correct.
sections.Issue: Did the CISG require consideration of the oral negotiations despite the writing and merger clause, and did the record establish that the printed limitations formed part of the agreement?
sections.Holding: Articles 8 and 11 required consideration of the relevant negotiations and circumstances. A genuine factual dispute remained over the shared intent to incorporate the printed terms and merger clause, preventing the requested judgment on the warranty claim.
sections.Reasoning:
The parties had places of business in different contracting states, the United States and Germany, so Article 1(1)(a) supplied the stated basis for applying the CISG. Article 8 directs attention first to actual intent known or necessarily apparent to the other party, and otherwise to the understanding of a reasonable person in the same circumstances. Its third paragraph requires consideration of negotiations, established practices, usages, and subsequent conduct. Article 11 rejects a general writing requirement in the circumstances addressed. The court therefore did not import the domestic parol evidence rule to exclude the oral account.

The merger clause did not prove its own adoption. The disputed assurances could support a finding that the seller’s agent knew the buyer understood the entire boilerplate section to be inapplicable. If both parties intended the written limitations to govern, Article 6 permitted them to vary the CISG’s default protections; if they did not, the printed warranty restrictions would fall away. This was a question for the factfinder. The opinion’s treatment of the CISG Advisory Council is an interpretive aid, not a claim that that private body enacts binding treaty law.

textbookImport.basis: Paraphrase of the exact supplied Fall 2026 Contracts Supplement; no subsequent-treatment review.

learning.why: TeeVee Toons makes the choice of legal regime concrete: the same dispute about a written agreement receives a different evidentiary analysis under the CISG than under the restrictive domestic approach in Gianni.

topics.assent: The parties’ understanding of the printed limitations determines whether they were adopted.
topics.cisg: Applies Articles 1, 6, 8, 11, and 35 to the international machinery sale.
topics.governing-law: Shows why the governing legal regime must be selected before using domestic evidence rules.
topics.parol-evidence: Declines to impose a domestic parol evidence barrier under Articles 8 and 11.
topics.interpretation: Considers negotiations and known intent, including intent concerning a merger clause.
topics.standard-forms: Boilerplate containing a merger clause cannot establish its own adoption.
topics.integration: The dispute turned on whether the printed merger clause made the quotation a final, complete writing, and the court held that under CISG Article 8 the parties' intent to adopt it was a fact question.
topics.warranty-overview: The claim rested on CISG Article 35(2)(a)-(b) fitness for ordinary and particular purpose, the Convention's counterpart to implied warranties, and on whether the fine print disclaimed them.
topics.cisg-framework: The entry's existing link uses the id 'cisg', which does not appear in the concept list; the atlas concept for the Convention is 'cisg-framework'.
